cues.text: Section seven: Enterprise IT evolution, five eras.
Enterprise IT means the technology used to support an organisation's operations and strategy at scale.
Its evolution is not simply a sequence of faster computers.
What changed over time was access, architecture, ownership and business models.
Let us go through the five eras in a table, taking one row at a time.
For each era, the table gives the architecture and use, the benefit, and the limitation.
First, the mainframe era, in the 1960s to 1970s, according to the dates in the LMS reading.
The architecture was a central computer with terminals, used for batch jobs such as payroll and census processing.
The benefit was large-scale, reliable processing.
The limitations were cost, the need for specialist access, and delayed results.
Second, the client–server era, in the 1980s to 1990s.
Here, departmental clients request services from servers, with local area networks and ERP systems.
The benefit was wider access and shared applications.
The limitation was the complexity of maintenance and scaling.
Third, the internet and web era, from 1995 to 2005.
The architecture was browser-based portals and e-commerce.
The benefit was global access and services available twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week.
The limitations were exposure to security threats and gaps in connectivity.
Fourth, the cloud and mobile era, from 2006 to 2016.
This brought on-demand infrastructure, software as a service, and smartphones.
The benefit was elastic capacity and mobile access.
The limitation was dependency on the provider and on the network.
Fifth, the digital ecosystem era, from 2016 onward.
The architecture is interconnected platforms, application programming interfaces, known as APIs, and data flows between partners.
The benefit is joint innovation and value creation.
The limitations are governance, privacy, and vendor lock-in.
A note on dates.
The lecture uses a broader range for the mainframe, from the 1960s to the 1980s, so these periods overlap.
Rely on the five-stage order and the defining architecture of each stage, rather than treating the boundaries as exact historical cutoffs.
Now let us look at each era in a little more detail.
The mainframe era was defined by batch processing.
Batch processing collects jobs and executes them together, for example payroll at month-end.
Users depend on central computing and on specialist operators.
In the client–server era, a client sends a request to a server, which performs a service.
For example, a desktop payroll application may access a shared database.
Computing and access spread across departments, although the service itself may still be centralised.
In the internet and web era, browsers and web servers make services available beyond office networks.
Customers can access a portal directly instead of visiting a branch.
Security and availability become more important, because exposure and service hours both increase.
In the cloud and mobile era, infrastructure can be provisioned on demand, and users can access applications on smartphones.
SaaS, or software as a service, means using provider-operated software as a service.
Elasticity means that capacity can grow and shrink with demand.
It is not a guarantee of low costs or of zero downtime.
In the digital ecosystem era, independent organisations connect services and jointly create value.
For example, a merchant can use a payment platform that connects banks and customers, rather than building every financial integration itself.
Now the tutor diagram.
Read it as a progression.
A central computer leads to networked clients and servers, which leads to web access.
From there, the path continues in two directions that follow the same line of development: cloud and mobile, and then partner platforms and APIs.
Finally, these models coexist today.
A bank, for instance, may retain a mainframe ledger while offering cloud-hosted mobile interfaces and partner APIs.
